question: How have attention mechanisms evolved over time?
preferenceReasons: Both trace the same core arc (Bahdanau → Transformer → efficiency → FlashAttention → GQA); A is fully reliable primary sources, while B adds helpful survey context but includes a likely fabricated/unverifiable 2026 arXiv link that offsets its broader coverage.

A covers the same primary arc (Bahdanau, Transformer, FlashAttention, GQA) as B but adds a taxonomy survey and a decade-spanning survey that tie the eras together and fill gaps (Luong, vision, sparse/linear, Mamba), though B is slightly more strictly primary-source-focused.

picks.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
picks.rationale: The original attention mechanism: Bahdanau et al. replace the fixed-length bottleneck vector in encoder-decoder RNNs with a learned soft-alignment over source positions, the additive-attention formulation everything later builds on.
picks.authors: Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, Yoshua Bengio

picks.title: Attention Is All You Need
picks.rationale: Vaswani et al. drop recurrence entirely and show scaled dot-product multi-head self-attention alone (the Transformer) beats RNN/CNN architectures while being far more parallelizable — the pivot that made attention the architecture, not an add-on.
picks.authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin

picks.title: Linformer: Self-Attention with Linear Complexity
picks.rationale: Represents the efficient-attention wave: Wang et al. show the attention matrix is low-rank approximable and project keys/values to cut self-attention from O(n²) to O(n), one of several approximation strategies (sparse, kernel, low-rank) of 2019–2021.
picks.authors: Sinong Wang, Belinda Li, Madian Khabsa, Han Fang, Hao Ma

picks.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
picks.rationale: Dao et al. shift the efficiency question from FLOPs to GPU memory traffic: exact attention via tiling between SRAM and HBM, delivering real wall-clock speedups where approximate methods failed — now the default attention implementation.
picks.authors: Tri Dao, Daniel Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra, Christopher Ré

picks.title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
picks.rationale: Ainslie et al. shrink the KV cache for inference by sharing key-value heads across query groups, getting near-multi-head quality at multi-query speed — the inference-side optimization now standard in LLaMA-style LLMs.
picks.authors: Joshua Ainslie, James Lee-Thorp, Michiel de Jong, Yury Zemlyanskiy, Federico Lebrón, Sumit Sanghai

agent.overview:
Attention began as a patch for a bottleneck: in 2014, Bahdanau et al. ("Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate") let a decoder soft-search over all encoder states instead of compressing a sentence into one fixed vector, inventing additive attention as a learned alignment mechanism. Three years later, "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017) turned the accessory into the architecture — scaled dot-product self-attention in multi-head form replaced recurrence entirely, trading sequential computation for parallelizability and giving us the Transformer.

Since then, evolution has been driven almost entirely by the quadratic cost of self-attention. The first wave (roughly 2019–2021) attacked FLOPs with approximations — sparse patterns, kernel methods, and low-rank projections like Linformer, which showed the attention matrix is low-rank and reducible to O(n). The second wave changed the metric: FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) observed that exact attention was memory-bound, not compute-bound, and used IO-aware tiling between GPU SRAM and HBM to get real speedups without approximation, quickly becoming the default implementation. The most recent thread targets inference rather than training: multi-query and grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) shrink the KV cache by sharing key-value heads, a change now standard in production LLMs. Read the papers in that order — Bahdanau for the "why," Vaswani for the "what," then Linformer, FlashAttention, and GQA as the three-stage answer to "how do we afford it."

picks.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
picks.rationale: The origin of neural attention: Bahdanau et al. replace the fixed-length encoder bottleneck with a learned soft alignment between source and target words, the foundational idea everything else builds on.
picks.authors: Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, Yoshua Bengio

picks.title: Attention Is All You Need
picks.rationale: The canonical primary source for the second era: Vaswani et al. drop recurrence entirely and build the Transformer solely on multi-head scaled dot-product self-attention.
picks.authors: Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin

picks.title: Attention? Attention! | Lil'Log
picks.rationale: Lilian Weng's widely cited survey taxonomy covers the whole pre- and early-Transformer landscape — additive vs dot-product, soft vs hard, global vs local attention, self-attention, NTMs, and the Transformer — making it the connective tissue between the primary papers.

picks.title: Not All Attention Is Equal: A Quantitative Survey of the EEI Trade-off
picks.rationale: A decade-spanning survey that traces attention from Bahdanau/Luong alignment through Transformers, vision, sparse/linear variants, FlashAttention, and Mamba, explicitly framing the evolution as an efficiency–expressiveness–interpretability trade-off.
picks.authors: Aditya Singh

picks.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
picks.rationale: Represents the systems era of the evolution: Dao et al. show exact attention can be made fast by tiling against the GPU memory hierarchy rather than approximating, reshaping how long-context models are built.
picks.authors: Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra, Christopher Ré

picks.title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
picks.rationale: Captures the inference-efficiency thread: Ainslie et al. introduce grouped-query attention, the head-sharing scheme between MHA and MQA that became standard in modern LLMs to shrink the KV cache.
picks.authors: Joshua Ainslie, James Lee-Thorp, Michiel de Jong, Yury Zemlyanskiy, Federico Lebrón, Sumit Sanghai

funnel.overview:
Attention began as a fix for a compression problem. Early encoder–decoder translators squeezed an entire source sentence into one fixed vector, and Bahdanau et al.'s *Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate* broke that bottleneck by letting the decoder softly attend to the relevant source positions at each step — attention as learned, differentiable alignment. *Attention Is All You Need* then took the radical step of discarding recurrence entirely, showing that self-attention alone (queries, keys, values, multiple heads, scaled dot-products) could carry sequence modeling, which made training massively parallelizable and birthed the Transformer era.

After 2017 the story splits into threads. Lilian Weng's *Attention? Attention!* maps the conceptual landscape between the two eras — additive vs. multiplicative scoring, soft vs. hard, global vs. local, self-attention — while *Not All Attention Is Equal* supplies the decade-long arc afterward, framing everything as a running trade-off among efficiency, expressiveness, and interpretability, from sparse and linear variants through vision Transformers to state-space competitors like Mamba. The dominant post-2020 thread is efficiency: *FlashAttention* shows the quadratic cost can be attacked exactly by respecting the GPU memory hierarchy rather than approximating the math, and *GQA* shows the KV-cache bottleneck at inference can be attacked architecturally by sharing key/value heads — the scheme now standard in production LLMs. Together the picks trace attention from an alignment heuristic, to the core of a general architecture, to a systems problem being engineered at the hardware level.

question: What are the main approaches to making LLM inference faster?
preferenceReasons: B covers all major threads (system-level serving, quantization, speculative decoding from the primary source, and architecture-level efficiency) with a full-stack taxonomy, while A omits the architecture-level approaches and leans on secondary surveys.

List A covers more of the topic's main threads—including the architecture-level approaches (linear/sparse attention, MoE) that B omits—while still hitting systems, quantization, and speculative decoding with less redundancy, whereas B overlaps its NVIDIA blog and speculative-decoding survey and narrows quantization to a single AWQ paper.

picks.title: Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization (NVIDIA Technical Blog)
picks.rationale: Clear engineering walkthrough of the prefill/decode split, why decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, and how KV caching, batching, and quantization map onto that bottleneck — the right mental model before anything else.

picks.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
picks.rationale: The vLLM paper: applies OS-style virtual memory paging to KV cache management, eliminating fragmentation so batch size (and throughput) can grow 2–4× at equal latency — the foundational serving-systems result.
picks.authors: Woosuk Kwon, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, et al.

picks.title: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration
picks.rationale: Shows that protecting the ~1% of salient weight channels identified via activation statistics enables 4-bit weight quantization with minimal accuracy loss, directly cutting the memory-bandwidth cost that dominates decoding.
picks.authors: Ji Lin, Jiaming Tang, Haotian Tang, Shang Yang, et al.

picks.title: Unlocking Efficiency in Large Language Model Inference: A Comprehensive Survey of Speculative Decoding
picks.rationale: Systematic survey of the draft-and-verify paradigm — where a cheap drafter proposes tokens the target model verifies in parallel — covering drafting strategies, verification/acceptance criteria, and variants like self-speculation.
picks.authors: Heming Xia, Zhe Yang, Qingxiu Dong, Peiyi Wang, et al.

picks.title: Inference Engineering, Chapter 5: Techniques (Baseten)
picks.rationale: Practitioner's chapter tying quantization, speculative decoding, caching, parallelism, and prefill/decode disaggregation into the production-serving picture, noting how quickly these techniques ship to real systems.

picks.title: A Survey of LLM Inference Systems
picks.rationale: Survey of production inference systems (vLLM, SGLang, Mooncake, DeepSpeed) covering scheduling, continuous batching, disaggregation, and distributed execution — useful for going from techniques to full systems.

agent.overview:
LLM inference is slow for a specific reason: generation is autoregressive, so each output token requires a full forward pass, and at small batch sizes that pass is bottlenecked not by compute but by memory bandwidth — the cost of streaming all model weights and the KV cache off HBM. Nearly every speedup technique attacks this fact from a different angle. The NVIDIA blog walkthrough builds this mental model first: the compute-bound prefill phase versus the memory-bound decode phase, and why the KV cache exists.

The approaches cluster into a few families. Shrinking the bytes moved: weight quantization (GPTQ, and especially AWQ, which shows you can hit 4-bit precision by protecting the small fraction of salient weight channels) directly cuts bandwidth per token, as does quantizing the KV cache. Wasting less memory: PagedAttention (the vLLM paper) borrows OS-style paging so KV caches don't fragment GPU memory, which lets continuous batching fit far more concurrent requests and lifts throughput 2–4×. Doing fewer sequential steps: speculative decoding has a cheap draft model propose several tokens that the large model verifies in a single parallel pass, converting serial decode steps into batched verification with identical output distribution. And at the systems level — parallelism, prefill/decode disaggregation, prefix caching, scheduling — the Baseten inference-engineering chapter and the survey of LLM inference systems show how these compose in production stacks like vLLM and SGLang. Read the NVIDIA post first for the bottleneck model, then PagedAttention and AWQ as the canonical system- and model-side wins.

picks.title: Full Stack Optimization of Transformer Inference: a Survey
picks.rationale: Systematic survey spanning the whole optimization stack — bottleneck profiling, hardware implications of LayerNorm/Softmax/GELU, fixed-architecture optimization, scheduling/mapping, and architecture search — giving the taxonomy every other pick slots into.
picks.authors: Sehoon Kim, Coleman Hooper, Thanakul Wattanawong, Minwoo Kang, Ruohan Yan, Hasan Genc, Grace Dinh, Qijing Huang

picks.title: Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization | NVIDIA Technical Blog
picks.rationale: Explains the fundamental prefill/decode asymmetry (decode is memory-bandwidth-bound) and walks through KV caching, MQA/GQA, FlashAttention, PagedAttention, parallelism, quantization, and speculative decoding as answers to that single bottleneck.

picks.title: Inside vLLM: Anatomy of a High-Throughput LLM Inference System
picks.rationale: A layered breakdown of how a state-of-the-art serving engine actually works — scheduling, PagedAttention, continuous batching, chunked prefill, prefix caching, speculative decoding, and multi-GPU scaling — connecting the techniques to a real system.

picks.title: Speculative Decoding: Exploiting Speculative Execution for Accelerating Seq2seq Generation
picks.rationale: The primary source for speculative decoding: a draft model proposes tokens that the target model verifies in parallel, yielding ~5x speedups with unchanged output quality — the key algorithmic lever for latency without accuracy loss.
picks.authors: Heming Xia, Tao Ge, Peiyi Wang, Si-Qing Chen, Furu Wei, Zhifang Sui

picks.title: Quantization I: Post-Training Quantization (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant) — The LLM Stack
picks.rationale: Builds the arithmetic behind why lower-bit weights directly speed up memory-bound decoding, then dissects the three essential PTQ algorithms (GPTQ, AWQ, SmoothQuant) and the activation-outlier problem they each solve.

picks.title: Speed Always Wins: A Survey on Efficient Architectures for Large Language Models
picks.rationale: Covers the architecture-level thread the other picks omit: linear and sparse attention, efficient attention variants, mixture-of-experts, hybrid models, and diffusion LLMs that reduce inference cost by changing the model itself.
picks.authors: Weigao Sun, Jiaxi Hu, Yucheng Zhou, Jusen Du, Disen Lan, Kexin Wang, Tong Zhu, Xiaoye Qu

funnel.overview:
LLM inference speed is governed by one central fact: autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound. Each generated token requires streaming all model weights (and the growing KV cache) from HBM, so the GPU idles waiting for data rather than computing. Essentially every optimization technique is an attack on this bottleneck from a different angle, and the picks divide into those angles.

The Full Stack Optimization survey maps the whole terrain from architecture to hardware, while NVIDIA's Mastering LLM Techniques post grounds it in the prefill/decode asymmetry and the standard toolkit: KV caching, MQA/GQA, FlashAttention, and parallelism. On the serving side, Inside vLLM shows how scheduling-level techniques — continuous batching, PagedAttention, prefix caching, chunked prefill — keep the GPU saturated by amortizing weight loads across many requests. On the algorithmic side, the Speculative Decoding paper introduces draft-then-verify generation, which parallelizes token production without changing outputs, and the LLM Stack quantization chapter explains why cutting weight precision to 4 bits nearly quadruples throughput in the memory-bound regime, via GPTQ, AWQ, and SmoothQuant. Finally, Speed Always Wins covers the architectural frontier — linear attention, sparse MoE, hybrid and diffusion models — where the model itself is redesigned to sidestep the quadratic and sequential costs entirely.

question: How do diffusion models work, and how are they used for video?
preferenceReasons: B covers both halves of the question better — an elementary tutorial and an annotated DDPM implementation explain how diffusion works from first principles, while a design-space survey plus the Video Diffusion, Stable Video Diffusion, and Sora papers cover video usage — whereas A leans heavily on primary papers without pedagogical support for the 'how they work' part.

List A covers all of B's key threads while adding a first-principles tutorial, a code-level walkthrough, and a survey of the video diffusion design space (3D U-Nets vs DiTs, training-from-scratch vs image-model adaptation), giving a technical reader a fuller and better-scaffolded path through the topic.

picks.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
picks.rationale: The canonical introduction of modern diffusion models: a fixed forward process gradually adds Gaussian noise to data, and a learned reverse process denoises it — with the key simplification of training via a denoising score-matching objective that yields state-of-the-art image synthesis.
picks.authors: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain, P. Abbeel

picks.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models
picks.rationale: Shows how to make diffusion practical at high resolution by running denoising in a pretrained autoencoder's latent space and adding cross-attention for text conditioning — the architecture underlying Stable Diffusion and most video diffusion systems.
picks.authors: Robin Rombach, A. Blattmann, Dominik Lorenz, Patrick Esser, Björn Ommer

picks.title: Video Diffusion Models
picks.rationale: The first strong extension of image diffusion to video: a 3D U-Net handles temporal coherence, joint image-video training stabilizes optimization, and conditional sampling extends clips in time and space.
picks.authors: Jonathan Ho, Tim Salimans, A. Gritsenko, William Chan, Mohammad Norouzi, David J. Fleet

picks.title: Stable Video Diffusion: Scaling Latent Video Diffusion Models to Large Datasets
picks.rationale: Demonstrates how latent video diffusion models are actually built and scaled: inserting temporal layers into a 2D latent diffusion backbone, finetuning on video, and — critically — systematic data curation, which the authors show matters as much as architecture.
picks.authors: A. Blattmann, Tim Dockhorn, S. Kulal, Daniel Mendelevitch et al.

picks.title: Video generation models as world simulators (Sora technical report)
picks.rationale: OpenAI's report on scaling text-conditional video diffusion via a Diffusion Transformer over spacetime latent patches, unifying variable durations, resolutions, and aspect ratios and producing minute-long coherent video with emergent simulation-like behavior.

agent.overview:
A diffusion model learns to generate data by reversing a gradual corruption process. Training takes a real sample, adds Gaussian noise step by step until it becomes pure noise, and trains a neural network to predict (and remove) the noise at any intermediate step. Sampling then runs this in reverse: start from random noise and repeatedly denoise until a clean sample emerges. This formulation, crystallized in "Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models" (Ho et al., 2020), turned out to be remarkably stable to train and produced image quality that beat GANs — the denoising objective is a simple regression loss, yet implicitly learns the score (gradient) of the data distribution at every noise level.

Two practical refinements made diffusion the dominant paradigm. First, latent diffusion (Rombach et al.) moves denoising from pixel space into the compressed latent space of a pretrained autoencoder, cutting compute by an order of magnitude while preserving detail, and adds cross-attention so the model can be conditioned on text. Second, for video, the core challenge is temporal coherence: "Video Diffusion Models" (Ho et al., 2022) extended the architecture to 3D U-Nets operating over frame stacks and showed that jointly training on images and video stabilizes optimization. Modern systems like "Stable Video Diffusion" insert temporal layers into a 2D latent diffusion backbone and finetune on video, with careful data curation proving as important as architecture. The current frontier, exemplified by the Sora technical report, replaces the U-Net with a Diffusion Transformer over spacetime latent patches — treating video as a sequence of patch tokens across time and space — which scales cleanly with compute and handles arbitrary durations, resolutions, and aspect ratios, yielding minute-long clips with surprisingly consistent 3D structure.

Read DDPM first for the foundational math and intuition, then Latent Diffusion to understand how everything is made tractable, then the Sora report for how the field now thinks about scaling video generation.

picks.title: Step-by-Step Diffusion: An Elementary Tutorial
picks.rationale: A first-principles tutorial on diffusion and flow matching that derives the training and sampling algorithms with only basic probability and calculus, deliberately avoiding SDEs and ELBOs — the cleanest foundation for how diffusion models actually work.

picks.title: The Annotated Diffusion Model
picks.rationale: Walks through the DDPM paper line-by-line with a complete PyTorch implementation, connecting the theory of forward/reverse noise processes to working code.

picks.title: Video Diffusion Models
picks.rationale: The primary source extending image diffusion to video: a space-time factored 3D U-Net, joint image-video training, and conditional sampling for temporal and spatial extension, with the first large-scale text-conditioned video results.

picks.title: Diffusion Models for Video Generation | Lil'Log
picks.rationale: A structured survey of video diffusion design space — 3D U-Nets vs DiTs, temporal consistency, and the two main routes of training from scratch versus adapting pretrained image models.

picks.title: Stable Video Diffusion: Scaling Latent Video Diffusion Models to Large Datasets
picks.rationale: Shows the practical recipe behind a state-of-the-art open video model: latent diffusion with a three-stage training pipeline (image pretraining, video pretraining, high-quality finetuning) and systematic data curation.

picks.title: Video generation models as world simulators | OpenAI
picks.rationale: OpenAI's Sora technical report describing diffusion transformers over spacetime latent patches and joint training on variable-duration video and images, framing scaled video generation as a path to world simulators.

funnel.overview:
Diffusion models generate data by learning to reverse a fixed noising process: a forward Markov chain gradually corrupts a sample with Gaussian noise until only static remains, and a neural network is trained to predict the noise at each step, so sampling means starting from pure noise and iteratively denoising toward a clean result. The picks ground this two ways — "Step-by-Step Diffusion" derives the math from elementary probability without SDEs or variational bounds, while "The Annotated Diffusion Model" ties the DDPM formulation to a working PyTorch implementation.

Video extends the same machinery with one hard extra demand: frames must agree across time, or you get flicker and identity drift. "Video Diffusion Models" is the canonical paper here, extending the image architecture to a space-time factored 3D U-Net with joint image-video training. Lilian Weng's post maps the broader design space — training from scratch versus inserting temporal layers into pretrained image models, and the shift from 3D U-Nets to diffusion transformers. "Stable Video Diffusion" then shows the modern latent-space recipe with staged training and careful data curation, and OpenAI's Sora report pushes the same idea to transformers over spacetime patches at scale, framing video models as world simulators. Together the picks cover theory, architecture, and the training practices that make video generation work today.

question: What is the state of the art in retrieval-augmented generation evaluation?
preferenceReasons: List A covers the canonical pillars of RAG evaluation—comprehensive survey, RAGAS, ARES, and major benchmarks (CRAG, RGB)—giving a technical reader the core landscape, while B, though containing valuable newer meta-evaluation work, omits RAGAS and a foundational survey and leans toward niche recent contributions.

Both lists anchor on ARES and a survey, but A better reflects the current state of the art with recent meta-evaluation (GroUSE), long-form/long-context evaluation (LONG²RAG), nugget-based scoring, and faithfulness-specific judges, while B relies more on foundational but older benchmarks like RGB and CRAG.

picks.title: Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey (Auepora)
picks.rationale: The most-cited survey of the RAG evaluation landscape; it proposes a unified framework (Auepora) that organizes metrics by RAG component — retrieval vs. generation — and by the output/ground-truth pairs available, then catalogs benchmark datasets, limitations, and open directions.
picks.authors: Hao Yu, Aoran Gan, Kai Zhang, Shiwei Tong, Qi Liu, Zhaofeng Liu

picks.title: RAGAS: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
picks.rationale: The de facto open-source framework for reference-free RAG evaluation, defining the now-standard LLM-as-judge metrics: context precision/recall, faithfulness, and answer relevance — usable without ground-truth answers.

picks.title: ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
picks.rationale: Finetunes lightweight LM judges on synthetic data to score context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance, using prediction-powered inference with a few hundred human labels to calibrate judge errors — the rigorous alternative to zero-shot GPT-4 judging.
picks.authors: Jon Saad-Falcon, Omar Khattab, Christopher Potts, Matei Zaharia

picks.title: CRAG — Comprehensive RAG Benchmark
picks.rationale: A 4,409-question Meta benchmark simulating web and KG search across dynamic, long-tail, and multi-hop facts; it exposed that strong LLMs top out at ~34% accuracy and simple RAG only reaches 44%, and it anchored the KDD Cup 2024 RAG challenge.
picks.authors: Xiao Yang, Kai Sun, Xin Luna Dong, et al.

picks.title: Benchmarking Large Language Models in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RGB)
picks.rationale: One of the first ability-centric RAG benchmarks, decomposing evaluation into noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness — a useful axis for diagnosing how models handle imperfect retrieved context.

agent.overview:
RAG evaluation has settled into a layered practice. At the core is a small set of LLM-as-judge metrics split by pipeline stage: retrieval quality (context precision/recall — did you fetch the right passages?) and generation quality (faithfulness — is the answer grounded in the retrieved context, i.e. no hallucination — plus answer relevance to the query). RAGAS operationalized this as a reference-free toolkit and became the industry default, while ARES pushed rigor further by finetuning small judge models on synthetic data and correcting their bias with prediction-powered inference using only a few hundred human labels — the right pattern when you need statistically trustworthy comparisons rather than a quick score. The open problems are well documented: judge reliability and position bias, the difficulty of scoring long-form or multi-hop answers, and whether component-level metrics actually predict end-task utility.

On the benchmark side, the field has moved from single-hop QA datasets toward stress tests of how models behave under realistic retrieval: RGB decomposes this into noise robustness, negative rejection, information integration, and counterfactual robustness, while Meta's CRAG benchmark showed how far we are from trustworthy factual QA — plain LLMs answer ≤34% of its dynamic, long-tail questions correctly and naive RAG only reaches 44%. Start with the Auepora survey ("Evaluation of Retrieval-Augmented Generation: A Survey") to get the full map of targets, datasets, and metrics, then read RAGAS and ARES for the two dominant practical paradigms (zero-shot LLM judging vs. finetuned calibrated judges), and close with CRAG or RGB to see what evaluation is actually measuring when it says a RAG system "fails."

picks.title: Can LLMs Be Trusted for Evaluating RAG Systems? A Survey of Methods and Datasets
picks.rationale: Systematic review of 63 papers organizing RAG evaluation across datasets, retrievers, indexing, and generators, giving the broadest map of current methodology.

picks.title: ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
picks.rationale: Canonical framework that finetunes lightweight LM judges on synthetic data to score context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance, with prediction-powered inference for statistical correction.

picks.title: The Great Nugget Recall: Automating Fact Extraction and RAG Evaluation with Large Language Models
picks.rationale: AutoNuggetizer revives TREC's nugget methodology with LLMs for automatic nugget creation and assignment, validated at run level against human judgments on the TREC 2024 RAG Track.

picks.title: LONG²RAG: Evaluating Long-Context & Long-Form Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Key Point Recall
picks.rationale: Benchmark plus Key Point Recall metric targeting the under-measured setting of long retrieved contexts and long-form answers across 10 domains.

picks.title: GroUSE: A Benchmark to Evaluate Evaluators in Grounded Question Answering
picks.rationale: Meta-evaluation benchmark of 144 unit tests across 7 generator failure modes showing that existing RAG evaluators, even GPT-4 judges, miss important failure modes.

picks.title: Benchmarking LLM Faithfulness in RAG with Evolving Leaderboards
picks.rationale: Vectara's industrial hallucination-tracking effort, introducing FaithJudge, an LLM-as-a-judge evaluator built on diverse human-annotated hallucination data to improve automated faithfulness measurement.

funnel.overview:
RAG evaluation has converged on reference-free, LLM-driven scoring of three core dimensions — context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance — and the current frontier is less about new metrics than about making those judges trustworthy. ARES established the template: finetune lightweight LM judges on synthetic labels and correct their predictions with prediction-powered inference against a small human-annotated set. The Great Nugget Recall takes a different, IR-rooted path, reviving TREC's 2003 nugget methodology — atomic facts that a good answer must contain — and showing fully automatic nugget creation and assignment agree strongly with human assessors on the TREC 2024 RAG Track. The survey "Can LLMs Be Trusted for Evaluating RAG Systems?" situates these within the wider landscape of datasets and component-level evaluation across retrieval, indexing, and generation.

The second thread is stress-testing the evaluators themselves. GroUSE meta-evaluates judges with 144 unit tests spanning seven failure modes and shows even GPT-4-based frameworks miss important failure types; Benchmarking LLM Faithfulness in RAG with Evolving Leaderboards brings an industrial angle with FaithJudge trained on human-annotated hallucination pools; and LONG²RAG pushes evaluation into long-context, long-form generation with its Key Point Recall metric. Together the picks divide into: the field map, the two canonical automatic evaluation paradigms (LM judges vs. fact nuggets), and the meta-evaluation and frontier-setting work that defines where the state of the art is still unreliable.

question: How do mixture-of-experts models route tokens, and what are the tradeoffs?
preferenceReasons: B covers all the core routing mechanics (top-k gating, Switch, expert-choice) plus more of the tradeoff threads—survey-level taxonomy, failure modes and modern fixes, and the systems/serving costs—while A's math note and DeepSeek paper overlap in scope with what B already covers more broadly.

Both cover the core routing mechanics (Switch, expert-choice, HF overview), but A adds a comprehensive survey and a systems-level analysis of serving costs, giving fuller coverage of the 'tradeoffs' half of the question, while B's added items (a math note, DeepSeek's balancing scheme) overlap with material already covered by its other entries.

picks.title: Mixture of Experts Explained (Hugging Face)
picks.rationale: The best single overview: walks through the lineage from Shazeer 2017 to Mixtral, explains top-k gating, load-balancing losses, capacity factor, and the inference-time tradeoff (high memory for all experts but low compute per token).

picks.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
picks.rationale: The canonical modern MoE paper: routes each token to a single expert (top-1), introduces the auxiliary load-balancing loss, capacity factor, and selective precision — the recipe most open MoEs still follow.
picks.authors: William Fedus, Barret Zoph, Noam Shazeer

picks.title: Mixture-of-Experts with Expert Choice Routing
picks.rationale: Flips the routing direction — experts choose their top tokens instead of tokens choosing experts — giving perfectly balanced loads and removing the capacity-factor tradeoff of token-choice routing.
picks.authors: Yanqi Zhou, Tao Lei, Hanxiao Liu, et al.

picks.title: Auxiliary-Loss-Free Load Balancing Strategy for Mixture-of-Experts (DeepSeek)
picks.rationale: DeepSeek's bias-adjustment scheme keeps experts balanced without an auxiliary gradient, avoiding the quality hit that balancing losses impose on the main objective — the approach used in DeepSeek-V2/V3.
picks.authors: Lean Wang, Huazuo Gao, Chenggang Zhao, et al.

picks.title: A Note on Sparse Mixture of Experts
picks.rationale: A compact mathematical writeup deriving how top-k routing and the balancing loss shape router gradients, plus coverage of shared/fine-grained experts and newer schemes like DeepSeek's controller and quantile balancing — good for the mechanics behind the tradeoffs.

agent.overview:
In a sparse MoE transformer, each feed-forward block is replaced by N parallel "expert" FFNs plus a small router — a linear layer producing a score per expert, softmaxed into gating weights. Each token's hidden state is sent to only the top-k experts (k=2 in Mixtral, k=1 in Switch Transformers), and their outputs are combined weighted by the gate. The payoff is decoupling parameters from compute: you can hold a 47B-parameter model but spend only ~13B parameters' worth of FLOPs per token. The catch is everything the router creates: routing is discrete and non-differentiable (gradients flow only through the gate weights, not the selection), and naive training collapses onto a few popular experts, wasting capacity and — worse — overloading those experts at serving time, since distributed MoE requires every token to land within each expert's fixed "capacity factor" buffer or get dropped/passed through.

This is why load balancing is the central design axis and the tradeoffs all live there. The classic fix, from Switch Transformers (Fedus, Zoph, Shazeer), is an auxiliary loss penalizing uneven expert utilization — but it fights the main language-modeling objective, and too much balancing pressure destroys expert specialization. Three camps have emerged: keep the auxiliary loss and tune it (Switch, GShard, Mixtral); restructure routing so balance is guaranteed, as in Expert Choice routing (Zhou et al.), where experts pick their top tokens instead of tokens picking experts, eliminating imbalance and token-dropping by construction at the cost of variable compute per token; or drop the loss entirely, as DeepSeek's auxiliary-loss-free strategy does, adding a per-expert bias term updated online to the routing scores so balance is enforced without contaminating the gradient of the main objective. Beyond balancing, the practical tradeoffs are: memory holds all experts even though compute uses few (bad for small-batch inference, great for throughput at scale), routing instability during training (mitigated by router z-loss and lower-precision gating), and expert granularity — newer models like DeepSeek use many fine-grained experts plus a shared always-on expert to get specialization without routing fragility.

Start with the Hugging Face "Mixture of Experts Explained" post for the full picture with worked examples, then read Switch Transformers for the foundational formulation, and Expert Choice plus the DeepSeek loss-free paper to see how the field resolved the balancing tradeoff. The "Note on Sparse Mixture of Experts" is the right reference if you want the gradient-level math.

picks.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
picks.rationale: The canonical primary source on modern sparse MoE routing: it simplifies top-k gating to top-1 switching, introduces the capacity factor and load-balancing loss, and shows how to train trillion-parameter sparse models stably at 7x speedups.
picks.authors: William Fedus, Barret Zoph, Noam Shazeer

picks.title: A Survey on Mixture of Experts in Large Language Models
picks.rationale: A systematic taxonomy of MoE covering router designs, load-balancing strategies, and system-level concerns like expert parallelism, with empirical comparisons across open-source implementations.
picks.authors: Weilin Cai, Juyong Jiang, Fan Wang, Jing Tang, Sunghun Kim, Jiayi Huang

picks.title: Mixture-of-Experts with Expert Choice Routing
picks.rationale: Explains the main alternative to token-choice routing: letting experts pick their tokens achieves perfect load balance and heterogeneous token-to-expert mapping, directly addressing the collapse/skew tradeoff of top-k gating.

picks.title: Mixture of Experts Explained
picks.rationale: A practitioner-oriented walkthrough connecting routing mechanics (top-k gating, z-loss, capacity factor) to the practical tradeoffs: faster pretraining and inference per FLOP versus high VRAM, fine-tuning difficulty, and communication costs.

picks.title: Training MoE Right: Making Every Expert Count
picks.rationale: Covers the failure modes of learned routing (expert collapse, uniform routing) and the modern fixes — auxiliary-loss-free balancing, shared experts, fine-grained segmentation, expert-choice — with a comparison table of the tradeoffs.

picks.title: Demystifying the Mixture of Experts Serving Tax
picks.rationale: Quantifies the systems tradeoff behind routing decisions: MoE models run 2–3x worse than FLOP-equivalent dense models in serving, and expert load imbalance that hurts prefill can paradoxically benefit decode.

funnel.overview:
Mixture-of-experts layers replace each feed-forward block with a bank of "expert" FFNs plus a small learned router: a linear layer scores every token against all experts, a softmax turns those scores into probabilities, and a discrete top-k selection sends each token to only one or a few experts whose outputs are combined weighted by the router scores. That sparsity is the whole point — parameter count (and thus capacity) scales with the number of experts while per-token compute stays roughly constant. The canonical design is "Switch Transformers," which simplified top-k routing down to top-1 and introduced the machinery everything since inherits: the capacity factor limiting how many tokens each expert accepts (with overflow tokens dropped), a differentiable load-balancing loss to prevent the router from collapsing onto a few experts, and z-loss-style stabilizers for training in low precision.

The tradeoffs live at two levels. At the training level, routing is learned jointly with the experts, so failure modes like rich-get-richer expert collapse or degenerate uniform routing are endemic — "Training MoE Right: Making Every Expert Count" catalogs the modern fixes (auxiliary-loss-free balancing, shared experts, fine-grained segmentation), while Google's "Mixture-of-Experts with Expert Choice Routing" flips the direction of assignment so experts pick tokens, guaranteeing perfect load balance at the cost of variable tokens-per-expert. The survey "A Survey on Mixture of Experts in Large Language Models" organizes this whole design space taxonomically. At the systems level, sparsity's FLOP savings are partly an illusion in practice: all experts must reside in memory and every MoE layer becomes an all-to-all communication across GPUs, which "Mixture of Experts Explained" covers from the practitioner side (VRAM, serving, fine-tuning difficulty) and "Demystifying the Mixture of Experts Serving Tax" quantifies rigorously, showing MoE serving runs 2–3x worse than FLOP-equivalent dense models with imbalance effects that differ between prefill and decode.

question: What techniques make large-scale training deterministic and reproducible?
preferenceReasons: B is more focused on training (A spends its flagship item on inference nondeterminism) and covers more of the topic's threads — RNG sources, floating-point order, distributed collectives, and cross-hardware verifiable training — with authoritative sources like the official Megatron deterministic-training docs and a NeurIPS paper.

List A concentrates on training at scale (Megatron's distributed determinism recipe, bitwise-auditable 1B run, cross-GPU verifiable training) while B spends items on inference batch invariance and the narrower gradient-accumulation quirk, making A more relevant to the large-scale training question.

picks.title: Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference
picks.rationale: Thinking Machines' writeup is the clearest explanation of the key insight — batch invariance: kernels (attention, matmul) that change their reduction order depending on batch size are the dominant nondeterminism source, and batch-invariant kernels eliminate it.
picks.authors: Horace He

picks.title: RepDL: Bit-level Reproducible Deep Learning Training and Inference
picks.rationale: Microsoft Research's paper systematizes the two sources of nondeterminism — RNG and floating-point accumulation order — and introduces deterministic kernel implementations achieving bit-level reproducibility across runs and platforms for training and inference.
picks.authors: Peichen Xie, Xian Zhang, Shuo Chen

picks.title: Bitwise-Deterministic Pretraining at Scale: How Megatron Core Finds and Removes Every Flipped Bit
picks.rationale: A practical postmortem on what nondeterminism actually looks like at thousands-of-GPUs scale: atomic adds, autotuner variance, and nondeterministic collective arrival order in NCCL, and how Megatron Core addresses each.

picks.title: ML Reproducibility on GPUs, in depth
picks.rationale: A comprehensive checklist covering floating-point reduction order, PyTorch determinism flags, seeded data pipelines, distributed gradient reductions, and how to verify results with a bitwise replay test.

picks.title: Reproducibility — PyTorch documentation
picks.rationale: The canonical reference for controlling randomness in PyTorch: seeding Python/NumPy/torch, cuDNN deterministic and benchmark flags, torch.use_deterministic_algorithms, and the documented limits of cross-platform reproducibility.

picks.title: PyTorch, Gradient Accumulation, and the dreaded lack of reproducability
picks.rationale: Shows a subtler source of irreproducibility: gradient accumulation changes batch composition and therefore numerics, so frameworks must handle it carefully to keep runs reproducible.

agent.overview:
Deterministic training fails for two independent reasons, and fixing it means fixing both. The first is randomness: weight init, dropout, data shuffling all draw from RNGs, so you must seed Python, NumPy, and PyTorch (and hash-derived seeds per sample in sharded data loaders) — the PyTorch Reproducibility note is the canonical checklist. The second, harder source is floating-point non-associativity: (a+b)+c ≠ a+(b+c) in fp32/fp16, so any reduction whose order is decided at runtime — atomicAdd in scatter/backward kernels, split-K matmuls picked by an autotuner, or NCCL all-reduce arrival order — flips bits run to run. Remedies are deterministic kernel variants (torch.use_deterministic_algorithms, CUBLAS_WORKSPACE_CONFIG, deterministic collectives), and, more recently, batch-invariant kernels: the Thinking Machines writeup shows attention/matmul kernels whose reduction order depends on batch size are the dominant source, and RepDL (Microsoft Research) implements deterministic kernels achieving bit-level reproducibility across runs and platforms.

At scale this becomes an engineering campaign: the Megatron Core postmortem walks through hunting down atomic adds, autotuner nondeterminism, and collective ordering across thousands of GPUs, while subtler traps remain — gradient accumulation changes effective batch composition and hence numerics (Mueller's post), so "same seed" isn't enough if the framework reorders work. The standard verification practice is a bitwise replay test: rerun a few steps and compare checksums. Read "Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference" first for the mental model, then the PyTorch docs for the flags, then the Megatron post to see how it plays out in a real large-scale stack.

picks.title: 5.8 Reproducibility and Inspection – Dive into Deep Learning
picks.rationale: Systematically inventories every source of randomness in a training run — weight init, dropout, data-loader shuffling, augmentation, parallel loader workers — and shows how seeding each generator plus layer-level inspection localizes the first divergent value.

picks.title: RepDL: Bit-level Reproducible Deep Learning Training and Inference
picks.rationale: Microsoft Research's open-source library that tackles the harder half of the problem — floating-point non-associativity — by enforcing correct rounding and order invariance to get bitwise-identical training and inference across diverse computing environments.

picks.title: Deterministic Training — Megatron Core
picks.rationale: The practical large-scale recipe: NVIDIA's Megatron documents exactly which environment variables (NCCL_ALGO=Ring, NVTE deterministic flags) and config overrides make distributed multi-node training bit-exact, and why collective-communication reduction order matters.

picks.title: OPEN-1B: A Fully Auditable Training Run
picks.rationale: Pushes determinism to its limit: imposes a definite order on GPU kernel reductions, data-parallel batch ordering, and inter/intra-node collectives so any single step of a 1B-parameter distributed run can be replayed bitwise on commodity hardware for independent audit.

picks.title: Optimistic Verifiable Training by Controlling Hardware Nondeterminism
picks.rationale: NeurIPS 2024 paper showing how higher-precision training, intermediate rounding, and shared rounding decisions via adaptive thresholding eliminate cross-GPU-type nondeterminism, achieving exact ResNet-50 replication across three different NVIDIA GPUs.

picks.title: ML Reproducibility on GPUs, in depth — Belgavi.AI Lab
picks.rationale: A practitioner's synthesis that frames reproducibility as three cost tiers, explains floating-point non-associativity from first principles, and walks through PyTorch determinism controls, seeded data pipelines, distributed reductions, and a bitwise replay test for CI.

funnel.overview:
Reproducibility in large-scale training decomposes into two distinct problems: controlling randomness and controlling floating-point arithmetic. The first is the easy half — every stochastic element (weight initialization, dropout masks, data shuffling, augmentation, even parallel loader workers) draws from a pseudorandom generator that a seed fixes, and "5.8 Reproducibility and Inspection" in Dive into Deep Learning catalogs these sources exhaustively. The harder half is that floating-point addition is not associative, so GPU kernels that use atomic accumulation or auto-tuned algorithm selection produce different rounding errors run to run even with identical seeds; the Belgavi.AI Lab writeup builds this from first principles and maps it to PyTorch's deterministic-algorithm controls and a bitwise replay CI test.

At scale, nondeterminism compounds across the system, and the picks divide that ground. Megatron Core's deterministic-training guide is the production recipe: pin the NCCL reduction algorithm (Ring, whose order is topology-fixed), force deterministic Transformer Engine paths, and set everything before the first cuBLAS call. RepDL attacks the general case with correctly rounded, order-invariant floating-point kernels for bitwise reproducibility across environments. Two research threads go further toward verifiability: "Optimistic Verifiable Training" eliminates cross-GPU-type divergence via higher-precision training with shared rounding decisions, enabling third-party audit, and "OPEN-1B" extends that to a fully auditable 1B-parameter run where any single step — kernel reductions, batch ordering, collectives — can be replayed bitwise on commodity hardware. Together these span the full stack: seed discipline, deterministic kernels, distributed reduction order, and cryptographic-grade auditability.

question: How do state space models like Mamba compare to transformers?
preferenceReasons: List A covers the comparison's core threads—foundations, the SSM-attention theoretical bridge (SSD/Mamba-2), the key copying/retrieval limitation, and empirical hybrid results—with only top-tier sources, while B includes lower-value or redundant items (a visual explainer and overlapping survey/theory papers) and misses the crucial limitation result.

B directly covers the comparison's core threads—foundations (Mamba), theoretical unification (SSD/Mamba-2), fundamental limitations (copying), and head-to-head scaling results—while A is broader but more diffuse with overlapping survey/tutorial items.

picks.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
picks.rationale: The foundational paper: introduces selective SSMs where state parameters are input-dependent (enabling content-based filtering), a hardware-aware parallel scan, and reports 5× higher inference throughput than Transformers with Mamba-3B matching Transformers twice its size.
picks.authors: Albert Gu, Tri Dao

picks.title: Transformers are SSMs: Generalized Models and Efficient Algorithms Through Structured State Space Duality
picks.rationale: The theoretical bridge: shows SSMs and attention variants are connected via semiseparable matrix decompositions, yielding the Mamba-2 architecture that is 2–8× faster than Mamba while staying competitive with Transformers.
picks.authors: Tri Dao, Albert Gu

picks.title: Repeat After Me: Transformers are Better than State Space Models at Copying
picks.rationale: The key limitation result: proves and empirically demonstrates that fixed-size-state models like Mamba are fundamentally weaker than attention at in-context copying/retrieval, the core tradeoff driving hybrid designs.
picks.authors: Samy Jelassi, David Brandfonbrener, Sham Kakade, Eran Malach

picks.title: On the Tradeoffs of SSMs and Transformers
picks.rationale: A high-signal conceptual explainer from a Mamba co-author's lab on the eidetic-memory (attention) vs. compressed-state (SSM) tradeoff and why neither family strictly dominates.

picks.title: An Empirical Study of Mamba-based Language Models
picks.rationale: NVIDIA's head-to-head scaling study showing pure Mamba underperforms on standard downstream tasks, and that a hybrid Mamba-Transformer-MLP architecture outperforms both Mamba and comparable Transformers at 8B scale.
picks.authors: Roger Waleffe et al.

agent.overview:
Transformers and Mamba-style SSMs differ fundamentally in how they remember the past. Attention keeps every previous token's key/value around, so it can recall anything from the context exactly — but at quadratic compute cost in training and a key-value cache that grows linearly during generation. A state space model instead compresses the entire history into a fixed-size recurrent state, giving linear-time training scaling and constant-memory, ~5× faster inference. The catch: a fixed state can't store everything, so plain SSMs were bad at content-dependent reasoning. Mamba (Gu & Dao) fixed much of that by making the SSM's parameters input-dependent — the "selective" mechanism lets the model decide per token what to remember or forget — and paired it with a hardware-aware parallel scan, producing a backbone that matches Transformers twice its size on language modeling. The "Transformers are SSMs" follow-up (Mamba-2) then showed attention and SSMs are mathematically two views of the same semiseparable-matrix structure, so the two families are far less distinct than the marketing suggests.

The real story is the tradeoff, not a winner. "Repeat After Me" shows attention is provably better at in-context copying and retrieval — exactly the tasks where eidetic memory matters — while NVIDIA's empirical scaling study found pure Mamba lags on downstream tasks but a hybrid Mamba/attention architecture beats both pure baselines, which is why production models (Jamba, Zamba, Bamba) are hybrids. Start with the Goomba Lab blog post "On the Tradeoffs of SSMs and Transformers" for the clearest conceptual map (compressed vs. exact memory), then read the original Mamba paper for the mechanics of the selective scan, and "Repeat After Me" for the honest account of where SSMs fall short.

picks.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
picks.rationale: The primary source: makes SSM parameters input-dependent for content-based selectivity and pairs it with a hardware-aware parallel scan, achieving linear-time modeling that matches Transformers on language.
picks.authors: Albert Gu, Tri Dao

picks.title: An Empirical Study of Mamba-based Language Models
picks.rationale: Controlled large-scale (8B) comparison from NVIDIA showing pure Mamba lags Transformers on in-context learning, but an 8:1 Mamba:attention hybrid matches or exceeds the Transformer baseline.

picks.title: Mamba-360: Survey of State Space Models as Transformer Alternative for Long Sequence Modelling
picks.rationale: Surveys the whole SSM lineage (S4, Hippo, Hyena, LRU, Mamba), its applications, and open challenges, giving the broader landscape beyond a single model.

picks.title: Theoretical Foundations of Deep Selective State-Space Models
picks.rationale: Provides rigorous grounding for why the selectivity mechanism lets SSMs rival attention, including theoretical links between gating, expressivity, and approximation.

picks.title: Jamba: A Hybrid Transformer-Mamba Language Model
picks.rationale: Demonstrates the practical synthesis: interleaving Transformer and Mamba layers with MoE yields 256K context, small memory footprint, and high throughput versus vanilla Transformers.

picks.title: A Visual Guide to Mamba and State Space Models
picks.rationale: An accessible, visualization-heavy walkthrough that builds intuition for SSMs and the selective scan step by step, explicitly contrasting them with Transformer attention.

funnel.overview:
Picks submitted. The core comparison comes down to a tradeoff: Transformers attend to every previous token with a key-value cache that grows quadratically in training compute and linearly in inference memory, while state space models compress the entire past into a fixed-size recurrent state, giving O(N) compute and constant memory. The catch, diagnosed in the original Mamba paper, is that earlier SSMs applied the same dynamics to every token and so couldn't do content-based reasoning; Mamba fixes this by making the SSM parameters functions of the input ("selectivity") and recovering efficiency with a hardware-aware parallel scan in place of the convolution trick.

The picks divide the ground across foundations, evidence, and practice. "Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces" is the canonical source for the mechanism itself, while "A Visual Guide to Mamba and State Space Models" builds the same intuition pictorially, and "Mamba-360" situates Mamba in the wider S4/Hippo/Hyena lineage. On the empirical side, "An Empirical Study of Mamba-based Language Models" is the most honest controlled comparison, showing pure Mamba lags Transformers on in-context recall but hybrids close the gap; "Theoretical Foundations of Deep Selective State-Space Models" explains mathematically why selectivity lets SSMs rival attention at all. Finally, "Jamba" shows where the field landed: production-scale models that interleave Mamba and attention layers to get long-context efficiency without sacrificing Transformer-style recall.

question: What are the best methods for choosing data mixtures for LLM pretraining?
preferenceReasons: B covers the full landscape (survey, offline optimization, scaling-law prediction, online adaptation, and empirical guidance on small-scale prediction) without redundancy, whereas A duplicates DoReMi via a blog post and includes the tangential DataComp-LM benchmark.

List A covers all major threads (survey taxonomy, offline proxy-based methods, mixing/scaling laws, online adaptation, and empirical decision guidance) with no redundancy, while List B duplicates DoReMi (paper plus blog) and includes the partly off-topic DataComp-LM.

picks.title: DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining
picks.rationale: The foundational method in this space: trains a small proxy model with group distributionally robust optimization to find domain weights that minimize worst-case excess loss, then transfers those weights to large-model training for a 2.6x speedup on The Pile.
picks.authors: Sang Michael Xie, Hieu Pham, Xuanyi Dong, Nan Du, Hanxiao Liu, Yifeng Lu, Percy Liang, Quoc V. Le, Tengyu Ma, Adams Wei Yu

picks.title: Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance
picks.rationale: Shows loss is a quantitatively predictable function of mixture proportions, fitting explicit 'mixing laws' on small runs to optimize the mixture before any large-scale training.
picks.authors: Jiasheng Ye, Peiju Liu, Tianxiang Sun, Jun Zhan, Yunhua Zhou, Xipeng Qiu

picks.title: RegMix: Data Mixture as Regression for Language Model Pre-training
picks.rationale: Formulates mixture selection as regression: train many small models on diverse mixtures, fit a model mapping mixture to validation loss, and simulate to pick the best — a cheap, general recipe validated at the 1B+ scale.
picks.authors: Qian Liu, Xiaosen Zheng, Niklas Muennighoff, Guangtao Zeng, Longxu Dou, Tianyu Pang, Jing Jiang, Min Lin

picks.title: Nemotron-CLIMB: CLustering-based Iterative Data Mixture Bootstrapping for Language Model Pre-training
picks.rationale: NVIDIA's approach for the common case where data has no clean domain labels: cluster the corpus in embedding space, then iteratively search the mixture space with smaller models, yielding state-of-the-art 1B-scale pretrained models.
picks.authors: Shizhe Diao, Yu Yang, Yonggan Fu, Xin Dong, Dan Su, et al.

picks.title: DataComp-LM: In search of the next generation of training sets for language models
picks.rationale: A controlled benchmark and testbed for data curation decisions (filtering, dedup, mixing) at fixed compute — essential for grounding mixture/curation choices in comparable evidence rather than folklore.
picks.authors: Jeffrey Li, Alex Fang, Georgios Smyrnis, Maor Ivgi, Matt Jordan, et al.

picks.title: Stanford CRFM: DoReMi — Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining
picks.rationale: A concise, well-written blog introduction to the DoReMi method and the intuition behind why data weighting matters, with an open-source PyTorch implementation — the fastest on-ramp before reading the papers.

agent.overview:
The core problem: pretraining corpora mix domains (web, code, math, books), and the proportions materially affect downstream performance — but historically labs set ratios by intuition and ablations that don't scale. The modern answer is to *predict* how loss varies with the mixture using cheap small-scale runs, then optimize the mixture analytically. Two main paradigms dominate. First, proxy-model methods: DoReMi (Xie et al.) trains a small model with distributionally robust optimization to find domain weights minimizing worst-case excess loss across domains, then trains the big model once with those weights. Second, regression/law-fitting methods: Data Mixing Laws (Ye et al.) and RegMix (Liu et al.) train many small models on varied mixtures, fit a function mapping mixture proportions to validation loss, and extrapolate to find the optimum — RegMix frames this as pure regression, Data Mixing Laws as explicit functional scaling laws, and both show small-scale predictions transfer to models orders of magnitude larger.

The frontier pushes on two limitations of those approaches. CLIMB (NVIDIA) addresses the fact that real web corpora lack clean domain labels: it clusters data in embedding space and iteratively bootstraps the mixture search with progressively larger models. Meanwhile DataComp-LM provides the controlled testbed that lets all these decisions — filtering, dedup, mixing — be compared at fixed compute, which matters because "best mixture" claims otherwise conflate data quality with proportions. Start with the CRFM blog post for a 10-minute intuition of DoReMi, then read the DoReMi paper as the canonical method and RegMix as the most practical general recipe; read Data Mixing Laws for the theoretical framing, and CLIMB if your data lacks domain structure.

picks.title: Rethinking Data Mixture for Large Language Models: A Comprehensive Survey and New Perspectives
picks.rationale: A comprehensive survey that taxonomizes data mixture methods into offline (heuristic, algorithm-based, function-fitting) and online families, giving the map of the whole field that the individual method papers slot into.
picks.authors: Yajiao Liu, Congliang Chen, Junchi Yang, Ruoyu Sun

picks.title: DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining
picks.rationale: The canonical algorithmic method: trains a small proxy model with Group DRO to find domain weights that transfer to a 30x larger model, yielding 2.6x faster training and +6.5 points few-shot accuracy on The Pile.
picks.authors: Sang Michael Xie, Hieu Pham, Xuanyi Dong, Nan Du, Hanxiao Liu, Yifeng Lu, Percy Liang, Quoc V. Le, Tengyu Ma, Adams Wei Yu

picks.title: Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance
picks.rationale: Shows model performance is a predictable function of mixture proportions, letting you fit 'data mixing laws' on small runs and optimize a 1B/100B-token RedPajama mixture to match 48% more steps of default-mixture training.
picks.authors: Jiasheng Ye, Peiju Liu, Tianxiang Sun, Jun Zhan, Yunhua Zhou, Xipeng Qiu

picks.title: Scaling Laws for Optimal Data Mixtures
picks.rationale: Derives scaling laws that predict loss as a function of model size, tokens, and the domain weight vector, extrapolating across scales and mixtures, and demonstrates this at large scale across LLM, multimodal, and vision pretraining.
picks.authors: Mustafa Shukor, Louis Bethune, Dan Busbridge, David Grangier, Enrico Fini, Alaaeldin El-Nouby, Pierre Ablin

picks.title: Adaptive Data Optimization: Dynamic Sample Selection with Scaling Laws
picks.rationale: The online counterpart: ADO adjusts the mixture during training using per-domain scaling laws of learning potential, with no proxy model or extra small-scale sweeps, matching or beating offline methods at lower overhead.

picks.title: How to Predict Best Pretraining Data with Small Experiments
picks.rationale: The DataDecide suite systematically tests which small-scale signals predict the best data at scale, finding single-small-scale ranking (~80% correct) is a strong baseline that 8 scaling-law methods fail to beat — essential guidance on how to make mixture decisions empirically.
picks.authors: Ian Magnusson, Nguyen Tai, Ben Bogin, David Heineman, Jena Hwang, Luca Soldaini, Akshita Bhagia, Jiacheng Liu, Dirk Groeneveld, Oyvind Tafjord, Noah A. Smith, Pang Wei Koh, Jesse Dodge

funnel.overview:
Choosing a pretraining data mixture means setting sampling weights over domains (web, code, books, etc.) on the probability simplex, and the field has converged on three families of solutions. The survey "Rethinking Data Mixture for Large Language Models" organizes these into offline heuristic, algorithm-based, and function-fitting methods, plus online ones. The classic algorithm-based approach is DoReMi, which trains a small proxy model with group distributionally robust optimization to find domain weights that transfer to models 30x larger — the proof that proxy-scale signals can set mixtures for frontier-scale runs.

The second family treats mixture choice as a curve-fitting problem: "Data Mixing Laws" and "Scaling Laws for Optimal Data Mixtures" both fit parametric functions predicting loss from mixture weights (plus model size and token count), so a handful of small runs suffices to compute the optimal mixture for any target domain and budget, replacing trial-and-error sweeps. The third thread, "Adaptive Data Optimization," adjusts weights online during training using per-domain scaling laws of learning potential, avoiding proxy models entirely. Finally, "How to Predict Best Pretraining Data with Small Experiments" (DataDecide) provides the empirical grounding: simple small-scale rankings already predict large-scale winners ~80% of the time, a baseline every fancier method must beat.

question: How does speculative decoding work and when does it help?
preferenceReasons: Both lists cover the core draft-then-verify mechanism and key variants without redundancy, but B better answers the 'when does it help' half by pairing a theoretical analysis of speedup limits and acceptance rates with concrete production constraints (TensorRT-LLM, HF docs), whereas A leans more on describing method variants.

B includes the foundational Leviathan et al. paper, the clearest practitioner explanation of when speedups occur (memory-bandwidth analysis), and the key Medusa/EAGLE variants, while A omits the seminal paper and substitutes more peripheral picks.

picks.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding (Leviathan, Kalman & Matias)
picks.rationale: The foundational paper: uses a cheap draft model to propose several tokens that the target model verifies in a single parallel forward pass, with a rejection-sampling scheme that guarantees the output distribution is identical to standard decoding — reporting 2-3x wall-clock speedups on T5-XXL.
picks.authors: Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, Yossi Matias

picks.title: Speculative Decoding — Inference Engineering (Baseten, Philip Kiely)
picks.rationale: A practitioner-grade chapter explaining why decode is memory-bandwidth-bound (so compute sits idle at low batch sizes), and how draft-token validation and acceptance rates translate that slack into more than one token per forward pass — the clearest source on when the technique actually pays off.

picks.title: Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads
picks.rationale: Replaces the separate draft model with extra decoding heads trained on the frozen backbone plus tree-based attention verification, removing the need to serve and align a second model while still yielding ~2x speedups.
picks.authors: Tianle Cai, Yuhong Li, Zhengyang Geng, Hongwu Peng, Jason D. Lee, Deming Chen, Tri Dao

picks.title: EAGLE: Speculative Sampling Requires Rethinking Feature Uncertainty
picks.rationale: Shows that drafting at the feature (second-to-top-layer) level with the target model's own sampled token is far easier than token-level drafting, producing the current strongest acceptance rates and speedups among open methods.
picks.authors: Yuhui Li, Fangyun Wei, Chao Zhang, Hongyang Zhang

picks.title: Unlocking Efficiency in Large Language Model Inference: A Comprehensive Survey of Speculative Decoding
picks.rationale: ACL 2024 survey that taxonomizes draft-model selection, verification strategies, and alignment requirements, useful for situating Leviathan-style, Medusa-style, and self-drafting variants in one framework.

agent.overview:
Autoregressive decoding is a serial loop: generating K tokens takes K forward passes, and each pass is bottlenecked by reading model weights from memory, not by compute — at low batch sizes the GPU's FLOPs sit mostly idle. Speculative decoding exploits that idle compute by making each forward pass do more work. A cheap "draft" model (or auxiliary heads) quickly proposes a block of γ candidate tokens, and then the large target model scores all of them *in parallel* in a single pass, since verifying a prefix is not serial the way generating it is. A modified rejection-sampling rule then accepts the longest prefix of drafts consistent with the target's distribution and samples a correction at the first disagreement — the key result from Leviathan, Kalman & Matias's "Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding" is that the output distribution is *exactly* that of the target model, so this is a pure speedup with no quality change, typically 2–3x.

When it helps is dictated by arithmetic, not hope: the speedup is roughly (expected accepted tokens per pass) × (verification is nearly free only while you're memory-bound). So it shines at small batch sizes, low-precision or memory-bound regimes, and when the draft and target agree often — easy, predictable text (code, translations, templated output) can see 70–90% acceptance, while high-temperature, high-entropy sampling drags acceptance down and can make speculation a net loss. At large batches the hardware becomes compute-bound, verification is no longer free, and speculative decoding can actively hurt throughput. The design space is mostly about where the drafts come from: Medusa attaches multiple decoding heads to the frozen backbone to avoid serving a second model, while EAGLE drafts at the feature level with the target's own hidden states for the highest acceptance rates to date; the ACL 2024 survey maps these variants. Read the Baseten chapter first for the memory-bandwidth intuition, then Leviathan et al. for the correctness guarantee.

picks.title: Unlocking Efficiency in Large Language Model Inference: A Comprehensive Survey of Speculative Decoding
picks.rationale: The broadest map of the field: gives a formal draft-then-verify definition, then taxonomizes drafter selection and verification strategies with comparative benchmarks — the anchor reference for understanding the technique's design space.
picks.authors: Heming Xia et al.

picks.title: SpecInfer: Accelerating Large Language Model Serving with Tree-based Speculative Inference and Verification
picks.rationale: The canonical systems paper: generalizes linear drafts to token trees verified in a single parallel pass by the target LLM, achieving 1.5–3.5× serving speedups while provably preserving output distribution.
picks.authors: Xu-Peng Miao et al.

picks.title: A Theoretical Perspective for Speculative Decoding Algorithm
picks.rationale: Answers 'when does it help' at the deepest level: via a Markov-chain abstraction it derives theoretical speedup limits and shows how the draft–target total variation distance bounds achievable acceleration, explaining why acceptance rate is everything.

picks.title: Speculative Sampling — TensorRT-LLM
picks.rationale: States crisply the two practical conditions for speedup — verification of many tokens must cost no more than one, and drafts must be accepted often enough — and catalogs production variants (draft-target, Medusa, EAGLE, n-gram, ReDrafter) as actually deployed.

picks.title: Assisted decoding — Hugging Face Transformers docs
picks.rationale: The hands-on entry point: shows speculative decoding as a one-argument change in generate(), and notes concrete constraints — assistant must share the tokenizer, be much smaller, and batched inputs are unsupported — that define when it helps in practice.

picks.title: SWIFT: On-the-Fly Self-Speculative Decoding for LLM Inference Acceleration
picks.rationale: Adds a thread no other pick covers: self-speculation via adaptive layer-skipping of the target model itself, eliminating the separate drafter entirely and yielding 1.3–1.6× training-free speedups — the plug-and-play end of the spectrum.
picks.authors: He-Ming Xia et al.

funnel.overview:
Speculative decoding attacks the core inefficiency of autoregressive LLM inference: tokens are produced one at a time, and at small batch sizes each forward pass is memory-bandwidth-bound, so running the model on many tokens at once costs barely more than running it on one. The trick is to have a cheap drafter — a small model, an n-gram lookup, or a lightweight head on the target itself — guess several future tokens, then let the large target model verify them all in a single parallel pass using rejection sampling that provably leaves the output distribution unchanged. Accepted tokens are committed; the first rejection triggers resampling from the target. The survey "Unlocking Efficiency in Large Language Model Inference" maps this whole design space formally, while SpecInfer is the canonical systems realization, extending linear drafts to token trees verified in one pass for 1.5–3.5× speedups.

When it helps is governed by one quantity: acceptance rate, which the NeurIPS theory paper shows is bounded by the total variation distance between draft and target distributions — the better the drafter agrees with the target, the closer you get to the theoretical speedup ceiling. Practically, the TensorRT-LLM docs spell out the two conditions (verification must be nearly free and drafts must be accepted often) and catalog deployed variants like Medusa, EAGLE, and n-gram drafting; the Hugging Face assisted-decoding guide shows the concrete constraints (shared tokenizer, much smaller assistant, no batching) for using it today. Two caveats matter: speedup evaporates at large batch sizes where the GPU is already compute-bound, and it shrinks when the workload is diverse or the draft–target gap is large — which is exactly what SWIFT sidesteps by self-speculating with layer-skipping inside the target model, no separate drafter or training required.

question: What are the main approaches to mechanistic interpretability of transformers?
preferenceReasons: List A covers more main threads (survey, foundational circuits framework, SAEs, a full circuit case study, frontier-scale circuit tracing, and methodology) with primary sources, while List B duplicates the monosemanticity thread, substitutes a secondary blog for the foundational circuits paper, and includes a dubious future-dated citation.

B covers all main threads — a field-wide survey, the foundational circuits framework, SAE feature decomposition, the canonical IOI circuit case study, modern circuit tracing, and practical tooling — whereas A lacks the original framework paper and an end-to-end circuit study, leaning more narrowly on the Anthropic/TransformerLens lineage.

picks.title: A Practical Review of Mechanistic Interpretability for Transformer-Based Language Models
picks.rationale: A comprehensive survey organizing the MI toolbox — feature discovery, circuit analysis, causal interventions (activation patching, ablation), and probing — making it the best single map of the main approaches.
picks.authors: Daking Rai, Yilun Zhou, Shi Feng, Abulhair Saparov, Ziyu Yao

picks.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
picks.rationale: The foundational circuits paper: it rewrites attention as a composition of QK and OV circuits, defines the residual stream as a communication channel, and identifies induction heads, establishing the vocabulary nearly all MI work uses.
picks.authors: Nelson Elhage, Neel Nanda, Catherine Olsson, Chris Olah, et al.

picks.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
picks.rationale: The seminal sparse-autoencoder paper showing that superposition-tangled neurons decompose into clean, monosemantic features — the basis of today's dominant feature-based approach to MI.
picks.authors: Trenton Bricken, Adly Templeton, Joshua Batson, et al.

picks.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
picks.rationale: The canonical end-to-end circuit case study, demonstrating how activation patching, path patching, and logit attribution are used to isolate and validate a full behavior-level circuit in a real model.
picks.authors: Kevin Wang, Alexandre Variengien, Arthur Conmy, Buck Shlegeris, Jacob Steinhardt

picks.title: Mapping the Mind of a Large Language Model (Circuit Tracing)
picks.rationale: The modern large-scale approach: cross-layer transcoders and attribution graphs replace MLP neurons so researchers can trace feature-level causal circuits in a frontier model (Claude Haiku 3.5).
picks.authors: Anthropic interpretability team

picks.title: 200 COP in MI: Techniques, Tooling and Automation (Neel Nanda)
picks.rationale: A practitioner-oriented overview of the methodological toolkit — ablations, patching, direct logit attribution, activation addition — plus the tooling (TransformerLens-style) needed to actually run these experiments.
picks.authors: Neel Nanda

agent.overview:
Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer what a transformer actually computes — turning weights and activations into human-understandable algorithms. The field rests on three pillars. First, the **circuits view**: "A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits" showed you can decompose attention into QK and OV compositions and treat the residual stream as a shared communication channel, which led to the discovery of concrete mechanisms like induction heads. Second, the **features view**: because neurons are polysemantic due to superposition, sparse autoencoders decompose activations into monosemantic features ("Towards Monosemanticity"), and this has scaled to frontier models via transcoders and attribution graphs ("Mapping the Mind of a Large Language Model"). Third, the **causal methods**: activation patching, ablation, direct logit attribution, and path patching are the experimental tools that turn hypotheses into verified circuits, as in the IOI study in GPT-2 ("Interpretability in the Wild").

Start with the "Practical Review of Mechanistic Interpretability" survey to get the full taxonomy, then read the circuits framework for the conceptual foundation and the monosemanticity paper for the feature-based paradigm; Neel Nanda's "200 COP in MI: Techniques" post is the hands-on companion if you want to run these experiments yourself with TransformerLens-style tooling.

picks.title: Micro-textbook: TransformerLens and Induction Heads
picks.rationale: A textbook-style treatment of the foundational 'A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits' paradigm — residual stream, QK/OV circuit notation, path decomposition — plus hands-on TransformerLens tooling, making it the best single grounding in the circuits approach.

picks.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
picks.rationale: The canonical circuits case study: reverse-engineers attention heads that implement prefix-matching/copying and presents six lines of evidence, including causal ablations, that induction heads are the mechanistic source of in-context learning.

picks.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
picks.rationale: Introduces the sparse autoencoder approach to resolving polysemanticity: learning overcomplete sparse features that are monosemantic, the foundation of the feature-decomposition thread of interpretability.

picks.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
picks.rationale: Shows the SAE method scaling to a production frontier model, extracting millions of features (including safety-relevant ones like deception and sycophancy) and demonstrating feature steering via causal clamping.

picks.title: How to use and interpret activation patching
picks.rationale: Best-practices guide to the core causal-intervention method (interchange interventions / causal tracing): experimental design, noising vs denoising, metric choice, and pitfalls in drawing circuit-level conclusions.

picks.title: Feature Superposition in Neural Networks: From Theory to Practice
picks.rationale: Surveys the theory and empirics of superposition — how networks pack more features than dimensions — and critically evaluates methods for recovering features, tying together the representational assumptions behind SAE-style work.

funnel.overview:
Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer transformers: rather than asking whether a model works, it asks what algorithm the weights actually implement. The field divides into three interacting threads. The first is circuits — decomposing the network into components (attention heads, MLPs) connected through the residual stream and explaining specific behaviors end to end. The mathematical framing of this, with its QK/OV decomposition of heads and path expansion of layers, is covered hands-on in the "Micro-textbook: TransformerLens and Induction Heads," while "In-context Learning and Induction Heads" is the flagship success story, tracing a concrete algorithm — induction heads doing prefix-matching — and arguing it mechanistically explains most in-context learning.

The second thread is feature decomposition, motivated by the obstacle that individual neurons are polysemantic: they respond to unrelated concepts because models pack more features than dimensions into superposition. "Feature Superposition in Neural Networks: From Theory to Practice" surveys this representational theory, and "Towards Monosemanticity" shows sparse autoencoders can recover clean, monosemantic features from activations — an approach "Scaling Monosemanticity" then demonstrates at frontier scale on Claude 3 Sonnet, including steering behavior by clamping features. The third thread is causal methodology: claims about what a component does require interventions, not just observation, and "How to use and interpret activation patching" is the reference for doing interchange interventions correctly — choosing metrics, baselines, and avoiding the pitfalls that make patching results misleading. Together these cover the field's arc: find the right units (SAE features), test their causal role (patching), and assemble them into verified circuits.
